title: One copy of the shared modules: merge oilpaint's and murex's spectral, spline, noise, reference, filters; Paint on Pigment
description: Supersedes murex-ant. A merge in both directions, not a re-pull. oilpaint has what murex lacks: the last-bit rounding fix in spline and noise (oilpaint #28: whole_floor, whole_ceil, WHOLE_SLACK, which live in oilpaint's _engine and must come down into the kit) and the guard that refuses kernels cached for another band count (oilpaint #22, spectral). murex has what oilpaint lacks: the compiled layer over a ground per pixel and paths that work out their dense points once (#5), spectral's stored tables (#9); murex.fusain depends on these. Then murex.huile imports the shared modules and its copies go; Paint becomes a murex Pigment plus body (Paint.mix, from_optics and pickles of older paints need care). oilpaint uses private names of spectral (_build_spectrum_to_rgb, _km_layer_batch, _layer_over_white; its tests read _BASIS, _CIE_1931, _CIE_WL, _D65_SPD, _D65_WHITE_XYZ, _RGB_TO_XYZ, _XYZ_TO_LINEAR_SRGB): inside one package that is no longer a public-API question. png: one writer, in the kit. The only step of the epic where pictures may move, and only fusain's (where the rounding fix lands in spline and noise): measure it; if hashes move, record them again with the images and say so in the changelog.
acceptance_criteria: tools/bench.py --compare identical on all 16 scenes; fusain's fingerprints identical, or the difference measured, explained and recorded; no module of murex.huile duplicates one of the kit; a test enforces the layers' import directions.
close_reason: One copy of the shared modules. huile imports murex's spectral, spline, noise, filters, reference and png; Paint is a murex Pigment with a body; oilpaint's rounding fix is in the shared modules (murex/_rounding.py). Measured: huile: bench --compare against oilpaint's last commit gives the same paint and picture on all 16 scenes, and its 8 example scripts rewrite 22 images with none differing. fusain: every hash of the fingerprint as it was, the thorough ones too (325 drawings, 12,037 marks); 12 of 16 example images byte for byte, 4 changed where a stroke's length was a whole number of steps (lake 116 px by 2/255 at most; macaw 0.42% of pixels, 46 at most; stilllife 0.24%, 28 at most; strokes 0.29%, 22 at most) and regenerated. 1855 tests pass, coverage 85.44%; tests/test_layers.py enforces the import directions.

Imports become murex.fusain; fusain's own version goes (murex's is the version). pyproject, tox, Makefile, CI, cspell and AGENTS.md take in what fusain's had (coverage omits for the compiled engine, the refcount and fingerprint conventions). Measured after the move: all 1031 tests pass; tools/fusain/fingerprint.py: 13 drawings, 493 marks, identical; tools/fusain/refcounts.py: nothing counted; all 16 example scripts run and no image of examples/fusain/output differs by a byte; coverage 94% of lines; the built wheel imports, mixes and draws. It now runs on murex's main (stored spectral tables, NumPy 2) where its lock had murex 0.2.0: no hash moved.

It keeps its own spectral, spline, noise, reference, png, _filters and paint for this step (deduplicated in the next), so that the move is a pure rename. Imports become murex.huile. It still carries its own copies of the shared modules (murex-9r5.3). Pickles made by oilpaint name oilpaint.* classes and do not load as murex.huile.*.

title: murex becomes the one package: murex.fusain, murex.huile, later murex.aquarelle
description:
Decided with the owner on 2026-11-18/19. One repository, one distribution named murex. The media are subpackages named in French after their flagship medium: murex.fusain (dry media, from the fusain repo), murex.huile (oil paint, from the oilpaint repo), later murex.aquarelle (wet media: watercolour, ink, markers). They are subpackages, not extras: every part needs the same numpy and numba.

Why: the goal is the most realistic simulation of any and all media, mixed. Support and medium are independent (watercolour on canvas, charcoal under oil, pastel on canvas), so no library boundary along either survives; media must in the end read and write one surface, which only works without lockstep releases in one package. Exactly one person uses these libraries, so names and versions are free to change.

Layers, imports pointing only downward: (1) colour: spectral and pigments, importing nothing else in the package; (2) kit: paths, noise, filters, Reference, image output, kept flat as murex.spectral, murex.spline, ...; (3) supports: papers and canvases; (4) surface state and render; (5) media, which never import each other and meet through the surface. A test enforces the directions.

Order: move first, deduplicate second, so each step is verified on its own (children of this epic). Not part of this epic: unifying oilpaint's Canvas and fusain's Sheet into one surface. That is a redesign to be made when the wet engine is written, against a shared surface from the start; dry media move onto it next, oil last.
close_reason: murex is the one package. murex.fusain and murex.huile are in with their histories (joce/murex#11), on one copy of the shared modules (joce/murex#13), with one tracker (joce/murex#14). huile paints what oilpaint painted, scene for scene; fusain's fingerprints are as they were, and four of its example images moved with the shared rounding fix. Not part of this epic and still to come: murex.aquarelle, and one surface that every medium reads and writes, to be designed when the wet engine is written.

title: huile: how far a knife drags wet paint depends on the step of the stroke
description:
Found in the review of murex-sdz. How high the blade rides is read once per step, from the wet paint under where the step takes it, which the heap it pushes has not reached yet: the longer the step, the lower it rides and the more it drags. Since murex-sdz the earlier paint moves as one column at full speed, and this shows more than it did.

Measured (18 configurations, steps cut 1, 2, 4, 8 times, 3 seeds): at a stroke's own steps against steps 8 times shorter, the dark carried along the pull (volume times distance) is +13 to +22% (+81% for a 60 px blade), where it was -3 to +11% before murex-sdz; the heap left at the end of the pull is +30 to +107% (+14 to +78% before; the default stroke +61% against +24%); the white laid is -8% at pressure 0.7, -12% at 0.9, +8% for a 160 px blade (-2%, -8%, +3% before). The paint under the pull is 1.5% thinner (2.4% at pressure 0.5). In very short steps the code before and after murex-sdz agree within 0.3%: the converged result is right, the stroke's own step is not short enough for it.

Tried in murex-sdz and left out: reading the level under where the blade stands as the step begins evens the thickness within 1% but sets the blade wavering at pressure 0.5 (0.10 units of ripple in steps up to 4 times shorter, where very short ones give 0.03).

Acceptance: carried paint, end heap and white laid within a few percent between a stroke's own steps and steps 8 times shorter, pressures 0.25 to 0.9, blades 60 to 160 px; no ribs (tests/huile/test_knife_steps.py); paint conserved. Alters the picture.
notes: Also in scope (review of murex-86z): light skims over wet paint. With murex-86z's fix and textures matched: thick dark base, load 0.3, step cap 2/8 = 0.912 at pressure 0.03 (worst seed 0.878), 0.938 at 0.05; white skimmed over an earlier wet white: 0.835 at cap 2, 0.775 at cap 1. With the blade resting on the canvas alone, all within 1.2%. Acceptance covers pressures 0.03 to 0.9.

title: Owner to provide: an image of a Bob Ross mountain, as the reference for huile's knife work
description:
The knife issues murex-dnj (snow that breaks in patches), murex-bja (ribbing), murex-sdz and murex-iaa came out of a look at one Bob Ross mountain, described by eye. None of them is to be worked on until a reference image is there to measure against: they all depend on this issue.

Needed from the owner (not something an agent finds or picks):
- an image of a Bob Ross mountain where the knifed snow breaks over the dark, sharp enough to see the holes (the one shown in the session that filed these issues was not kept: an upload does not survive a cloud session);
- where it is to live: in the repository (examples/huile/reference, in Git LFS, committed from a machine with git-lfs; the painting is under copyright, unlike the old masters there, so that is the owner's decision) or outside it, with only the measurements recorded here.

Then, before closing this: measure a crop of the snow face (share covered, sizes of the holes, how far they stretch along the pull, thickness of the white between them if the image shows it) and write the numbers into murex-dnj as its acceptance targets.

title: huile: ribbing under a knife as stick-slip of stiff paint, not of the step
notes: The snow issue is murex-dnj. The ripple against body is measured by: python tools/huile/knife_probe.py ribs.

title: huile: a skimming knife breaks in patches, as Bob Ross lays snow on a mountain
description:
Bob Ross lays snow with one or a few pulls of a knife carrying a small roll of stiff white, with almost no pressure, over a thin wet dark. The paint does not go on evenly: it "breaks", leaving holes where the dark shows as bare rock. The holes are many threads wide, ragged, stretched along the pull; the white between them is at full thickness with crisp edges.

What huile does today (_knife._slab, pressure under about 0.3): the bead on the blade's edge lays paint on each pixel in proportion to how far the surface reaches into it, where the canvas threads and the blade's nicks stand high. Tested (white over wet dark, pressures 0.03 to 0.25, loads 0.3 to 8), it gives:
- a speckle the size of one thread, aligned to the weave (a halftone screen on the default canvas);
- long parallel streaks from the nicks and from running dry;
- either a whole slab or speckle, never solid islands with ragged holes;
- on LINEN_COARSE with irregularity 1 and an uneven base, a less regular speckle, still thread-sized.
examples/huile/bob_ross_style.py shows it: its snow is mostly solid smears.
Caveat: the dark base of these tests was 2.3 to 2.9 units thick, not a thin scraped film. Redo them over a thin base first.

What seems to be missing (a reading of the mechanics, not measured), none of it a flow solver:
1. Transfer that sticks or does not, with memory along the stroke: where the roll touches it tears off as a lump; laying keeps laying (the paint's cohesion) until the surface dips or the roll runs out there; broken stays broken until something catches. Easier to go on than to start.
2. The bead tracked along the blade's edge: each place on the edge has its own supply, used up where it lays and evened out sideways only slowly, so a hole follows a patch. (The skim rule seems to use one film per step: _film not traced to confirm.)
3. Relief at scales above the weave, several threads to a few centimetres: the uneven thickness of the underlayer, the give of a stretched canvas, the hand.

Acceptance: a mountain face as in the reference (dark base knifed thin, one or two skimmed pulls of white) breaks in patches, measured by the size distribution and elongation of the holes and by the thickness of the white between them, not by eye alone; the same with the stroke cut into finer steps; paint conserved.

Alters the picture: bench scenes and every image of examples/huile/output regenerated, bob_ross_style.py reworked to use it.
notes: Ribbing is murex-bja; the per-step ridge is murex-sdz. The tests are kept as: python tools/huile/knife_probe.py skim --save DIR (the grid of pulls by pressure and load; --base 1 for a thin dark base).

title: huile: a knife dragging wet paint leaves a ridge at every step of the stroke
notes: Measured by: python tools/huile/knife_probe.py ribs (the table by body, with the film drag on and off; --save DIR for the pictures). The step was halved by hand, the cap in stroke.py.
close_reason: The earlier paint under the blade moves as one column, and the blade fills the gap it meets as it goes. What it costs: murex-kau (drag depends on the step), murex-6fa (lumps).

title: The media's kernels and noise.py follow the machine's maths library, as the colour science no longer does
description: murex-krb made the colour science give the same bits on every machine: no NumPy transcendental, no math function in a kernel, no BLAS product (see AGENTS.md and murex/_libm.py). The rest of what makes a picture does not hold to it yet. huile's kernels call math.exp (25 times in _engine.py), math.log1p, math.cos, math.tan, math.atan2, and powers with ** (0.8, 1.2, 1.5, soft_pow); its renderer np.tanh; _dab.py np.sin, np.cos, math.hypot and ** 0.6; fusain's engine math.exp, math.atan2, math.sin, math.cos, math.hypot and ** 1.5; murex/noise.py np.sin and non-integer powers (the paper and canvas textures). numba sends math functions to the C library, which differs between systems and, with fused multiply-add, between processors; NumPy's sin, cos, exp and power take SIMD paths that round per processor. So a picture may still differ in its last bits from one machine to another, and the media check theirs byte for byte. Measure first: the ARM CI job (added with murex-krb) runs the media's tests; see whether fusain's fingerprints and huile's tests hold there. Then move what differs onto murex._libm (adding sin, cos, atan2, log1p, hypot as needed), each move a breaking change that records the pictures again.
acceptance_criteria: Either the media's pictures are shown to be the same on ARM and x86-64 (closed with the evidence), or their kernels and noise use murex._libm and the ARM job runs every test.
notes: 21 Nov 2026, measured on the first ARM CI run (ubuntu-24.04-arm, joce/murex#19, job 136709223603): every pin of the colour science held there (tests/test_bits.py, tests/test_libm.py), and all 13 drawings of fusain's recorded fingerprint differed: tests/fusain/test_fingerprint.py skipped them (it skips, rather than fails, when the machine's arithmetic hash is not that of the recording machine). So fusain's pictures do follow the machine, through its own kernels (math.exp, math.atan2, math.sin, math.cos, math.hypot, powers), since its colours no longer do. huile's tests passed on ARM, but none pins its pictures; tools/huile/bench.py --compare between an x86 and an ARM run would tell. Raised to P2: the media are what the pictures are made of.
close_reason: Not doing. Identical bits on every machine was built and worked (joce/murex#19 for the colour science, merged then reverted; joce/murex#21 for the media, CI green on x86-64, ARM and Windows, closed unmerged), but it takes murex's own maths library (fdlibm ports, about 900 lines), NumPy's ziggurat tables for the random draws, and a ban on ordinary NumPy calls in murex's code. The owner judged that not worth it for this project. Pictures are checked to the bit on one machine; on another kind of machine the recorded hashes are skipped. AGENTS.md says so, and says not to bring it back unasked. The work stays reachable from joce/murex#21.

title: One set of tooling and one tracker; archive the fusain and oilpaint repositories
description: One AGENTS.md with each engine's conventions, and the ones that belong to all kernels made general (oilpaint's last-bit rounding rule, fusain's no-refcount rule: check whether each holds in the other engine). One README that presents the package and its media. One changelog going forward, the two old ones kept as history. Open issues of fusain (fusain-586, fusain-fdh) and oilpaint brought here (check whether bd import takes issues with another prefix; otherwise recreate the open ones and name the old ids). A final note in each old repository's README pointing here; then the owner archives both on GitHub (oilpaint 0.1.0 stays on PyPI as it is). Publishing a murex release is asked for separately.
acceptance_criteria: No open issue is left only in an old repository; both old READMEs point to murex; the owner has been asked to archive.
close_reason: One tracker and one set of tooling. The open issues of the old trackers are here (fusain-586 is murex-1gp, fusain-fdh is murex-6wh, oilpaint-76t is murex-252; joce/murex#14). Both old READMEs open with a notice that the library has moved (joce/fusain#87, joce/oilpaint#30), their open issues are closed as moved, and Dependabot's configuration is removed from both (joce/fusain#88, joce/oilpaint#30). The owner has been asked to archive both repositories, which only they can do; three Dependabot pull requests are left open there (joce/oilpaint#13, joce/fusain#85, joce/fusain#86), for the owner to close or leave frozen. Whether huile's kernels count references is murex-bz2.

title: make pre-push takes too long: the suite runs six times, one process each
description: make pre-push runs tox's whole envlist (black, ruff, pyright and pytest on five Python versions, one after another), then the suite a sixth time for coverage. Measured on 4 cores: fusain's suite takes 173 s per run and oilpaint's 162 s, so pre-push spends 20 minutes or more in each. CI already runs the versions in parallel jobs. Fix: run the tests with pytest-xdist (-n auto) and have pre-push check once, on the current Python (lint env, coverage, wheel, spell-changed); make tox keeps the full matrix.
close_reason: pytest-xdist (-n auto) in every tox env that runs the tests, and make pre-push runs lint (black, ruff, pyright), coverage and spell-changed once on the current Python instead of tox's whole envlist plus coverage. make tox keeps every version and the wheel, as CI does. Measured on 4 cores: murex 19 s.

title: A compiled layer over a ground for each pixel; a path that works out its dense points once
description: fusain made its drawings faster by working round murex in two places: its own compiled copy of km_layer for a layer over a ground that differs per pixel (km_depth, km_over), and a Path subclass that keeps its dense points (_Dense). Both belong here. km_layer hands a batch of plain float64 layers, over one ground or a ground for each, to compiled kernels (and takes out=, which may be the ground); a Path keeps its dense points until its control points change, and the dense points of a CatmullRom, the arc lengths and the tangents are compiled. Not a breaking change: every result is what 0.1.1 gave, to the bit, which tests/test_exact.py checks against the code of 0.1.1.
close_reason: Done. A layer over a ground per pixel on 1120x820: 790-830 ms in numpy, 147-152 ms compiled (fusain's own copy: 153). A short stroke's path made, sampled and asked its length: 248 us, now 24 us. Bit for bit against the code of 0.1.1 (tests/test_exact.py; numpy 1.24, 1.26, 2.0, 2.4, 2.5) and fusain's thorough fingerprint (325 drawings), with fusain as it is and with fusain calling murex instead of its copies. oilpaint was not run: it is not on murex yet (murex-ant), and its tools/bench.py --compare must be run when it moves.

title: fusain: pastel pencils (pastels.pencil)
description:
A pastel pencil is a hard-pastel core in a wooden casing: sharpened to a fine point for detail, its side is the bared cone of the core (darkest down the middle, fading to the edges) rather than a stick laid flat. The core is about as hard as a hard pastel or a little harder, with a little more binder, so it dusts a little less. It has no wax: it layers, blends with a finger and erases as a pastel does.

fusain can already draw one: pastels.hard(c).with_(flat_side=False, side=SIDE, ...) held in a Stick with a small width. This issue adds the preset, pastels.pencil(color, name=None), so that nobody has to know which fields to change, with defaults for its softness and binding (between pastels.hard and a coloured pencil's, guessed until measured against a real one) and a suggested point width in its docstring or a helper.

Not part of it: brittle cores that snap under hard pressure (that would be a Stick behaviour shared by every pastel), and water-soluble pastel pencils (CarbOthello), which belong with murex.aquarelle.
acceptance_criteria: pastels.pencil exists, documented like soft/hard/oil; flat_side False and the pencil's side; tests that its tilted band fades to its edges as a pencil's does, that it dusts less than pastels.hard, and that the medium is conserved; no change to fingerprints or existing images.

title: fusain: Conté crayons and the chalk colours (sanguine, sepia, bistre, white)
description:
Add the classic drawing chalks as fusain media, probably a new module (murex/fusain/conte.py, or presets in pastels.py). A Conté crayon is a square stick of pigment, clay and a little binder, between a hard pastel and compressed charcoal: firmer than a hard pastel, dusts less, holds a sharp edge, smudges less under a finger, and erases less cleanly. Sanguine (red iron oxide), sepia, bistre and white chalk are its classic colours; with black they make the trois crayons technique on toned paper (papers.TONED_TAN, papers.TONED_GREY already exist).

What is needed: pigments for sanguine, sepia, bistre, white and black (iron-oxide earths are opaque and fairly weak; white must cover on tan paper); Medium values (softness, binding, flat_side=True with a square stick's side, no wax, no sheen); and an example drawing in examples/fusain/ in trois crayons on toned paper.

Mostly presets: no new mechanism is expected. If the clay should make it lay paler or take worse on top of itself than a pastel does, that is a measurement against real Conté first, not a new field.
acceptance_criteria: Conté presets (at least black, sanguine, sepia, white) with docstrings saying how each behaves; tests that they lay, smudge less than a soft pastel and conserve the medium; an example in examples/fusain/ with its image (in LFS); fingerprints and existing images unchanged, since no existing medium changes.

title: huile: a stroke's textures depend on how it is cut into steps
description:
Found in murex-86z and confirmed in its review. A stroke's width wobble counts its noise in samples (stroke.py: value_noise_1d(len(pts)+2, 0.8*w/spacing)), so a stroke cut into finer steps draws more random numbers, and every texture drawn after it (blade tilt, bands) differs. With real draws a light skim cut 4 times finer leaves 0.83 to 1.51 times as much, and with the step cap at 2, 0.94 to 1.21: as much as from seed to seed (7.6% on average, up to 16%). With the draw counts matched, cutting finer either way gives the same within 1.3%.

So a stroke shows how it is cut into steps through its random textures, and any test comparing step lengths must match the draws or average seeds.

Brushes: _engine.own_lift uses the nominal step the same way the skim bead did before murex-86z (0.4 + 2h/K.spacing), and brush strokes depend on the step (cap 2: 0.85 to 1.08). Not attributed; measure it here or file it apart.

Fix: textures drawn against distance along the path, with a count of draws that does not depend on the step. Alters every picture of huile (all bench scenes, all example images): a breaking change; decide whether it is worth it. Acceptance: the same stroke at step caps 8, 4, 2 has the same textures (same wobble, tilt and bands along its length), measured, not by eye.

title: huile: a loaded knife pull along an earlier pull's end ridge drops tall lumps
description:
Found in murex-sdz and measured in its review. On the dark ground of tools/huile/knife_probe.py ribs (vertical 160 px knife pulls, load 5, pressure 0.7, each overlapping the ridge the earlier one left at its blade's end), the ridge is bulldozed into a heap and dropped as a lump about 10 units high on paint 3.5 thick. Pixels above 8 units, before -> after murex-sdz: 420x300, body 0.2: 0 -> 34; body 0.7: 18 -> 48; 900x500: 10 -> 36 and 39 -> 118. In steps 4 times shorter, body 0.7: 9 -> 18 and 75 -> 127. Rendered: 2 to 4 more small glints per dark ground. Not seen in the bench scenes nor in crossing pulls.

The new flow of murex-sdz (the column moving as one) gathers the ridge whole; the lump-making itself is older and depends on the step (before: 18, 1, 9 pixels at steps 1, 1/2, 1/4). Which rule releases the heap is not traced; the author of murex-sdz names the rule that the blade stops dragging under its own slab thicker than 0.3 (unverified).

Acceptance: trace what releases the heap; a pull along an earlier ridge spreads it or carries it without leaving isolated peaks, the same at a stroke's steps and at finer ones; paint conserved. Alters the picture.

title: huile: what a skimming knife's bead lays depends on the step of the stroke
description:
Found in the review of murex-iaa. With the step cap of stroke.py (8 px) set to 4 and 2, a light pull of a heavily loaded knife leaves more paint: on the bare canvas at pressure 0.03, load 8, 18.8k -> 26.3k -> 32.0k (x1.70 at cap 2); load 3, x1.43; at pressure 0.08, load 8, x1.28. At pressures 0.15 and 0.25 it is x1.00. A stroke must not show how it is cut into steps.

Where it comes from, measured by the reviewer: mostly the nominal step in the bead's own rule, not the stepping. K.spacing (the cap) enters n = 0.4 + 2h/K.spacing in _knife._slab, and pass_bead = n(1 - exp(-4/n)) grows as the cap shrinks. With n's spacing held at 8 while stepping at 2 the ratios fall to x1.11 (p 0.03, load 8), x1.10 (load 3), x1.04 (p 0.08, load 8). The remaining 4 to 11% is not traced (a guess: the bead's touch grows as the stroke's own paint builds up during a pass).

Before murex-iaa this regime laid nothing, so it did not show; the old code had the same dependence elsewhere (x1.79 at p 0.08, load 1).

murex-dnj reworks the bead's accounting (a supply tracked along the edge): fix this there or before it. Acceptance: the volume a skimmed pull leaves is the same within a few percent with the step cap at 8, 4 and 2, pressures 0.03 to 0.25, loads 0.3 to 8; paint conserved.
close_reason: The bead's pass count uses a fixed length, and its touch reads the surface without the stroke's own paint. What is left over wet paint is murex-kau's.

title: Examples: their own maths still differs by machine
description: The example scripts (examples/huile/*.py, examples/fusain/*.py) compute their own inputs with NumPy's np.sin, np.cos, np.interp, np.arctan2, ** to fractions and rng.normal (whose loc + scale*z NumPy may fuse on ARM). murex itself is the same everywhere (murex-9v4), but an example regenerated on ARM or Windows may differ from the committed image in its last bits. Use murex._libm / murex._random there too, or expose a small public API for scripts (murex.sin? a murex.random module?) so that a user's own scripts can be the same everywhere. Decide whether that API is wanted first.
close_reason: Moot: murex._libm and murex._random are not kept (joce/murex#21 closed, joce/murex#19 reverted; see murex-9v4).

title: huile: a knife barely touching lays less the more paint it carries
notes: Measured by: python tools/huile/knife_probe.py skim (volume left by each pull, by pressure and load). It holds over a thin base too (--base 1): at pressure 0.03, load 0.3 leaves 3177, load 1 leaves 15.5, load 3 leaves 0.0, load 8 leaves 1015; at 0.08 they leave 3221, 5909, 14547 and 33994. Over the thick base (--base 5): 3141, 398, 1.1, 1015 at 0.03.
close_reason: The bead hangs from the level the blade would ride at on no more paint than the bead. Step dependence it exposed: murex-86z.

title: Check whether huile's kernels count references as they work, as fusain's must not
description: fusain found that numba counts a reference wherever an array is handed to a helper under an `if` or after an early `return`, and that the counting doubles the time of a stroke and nearly triples that of a rub (top of murex/fusain/_engine.py; tools/fusain/refcounts.py tells what is still counted, tests/fusain/test_refcounts.py fails if anything is). huile's engine (murex/huile/_engine.py, 6,300 lines of kernels) was never looked at this way: it was a library of its own until murex-9r5. Run the same inspection on its kernels (the tool reads the compiled IR; it names fusain's kernels, so it needs to be told huile's or made general and moved to tools/), and say what is counted and in which kernels. If much is, removing it is an optimisation that must leave tools/huile/bench.py --compare identical on all 16 scenes, timed with tools/huile/bench.py before and after. Named in murex-9r5.4 as the one of each engine's rules not yet checked against the other (huile's rounding rule became murex's in murex-9r5.3).
acceptance_criteria: What huile's kernels count is measured and written here. Either nothing worth removing (closed with the numbers), or an issue for the removal with the expected gain.
close_reason: Measured: nothing worth removing. (1) What is counted, from the LLVM of huile's 130 kernels compiled afresh (fusain's tools/fusain/refcounts.py analysis, told the modules _engine, _render, _dab): 2,197 counts outside loops and 414 inside them, most in deposit (119 inside loops), flow_under_blade (64), pull_up (44), lay_ridges_off (39), level (28); 60 kernels count nothing. (2) Where the time goes: timing each kernel Python calls over the 16 scenes of tools/huile/bench.py, brush_step (one call per brush step, the rest compiled into it) is about 94% of it; then level, flow_under_blade, soften, fix_coverage, each under 9%. (3) What the counting costs: the whole benchmark (best of 5) built with numba's counts made plain load-add-store instead of atomic (same counts, same frees; patching numba.core.runtime.nrtdynmod._define_atomic_inc_dec, each build compiled afresh) against two normal builds: 18.40 s plain, 19.39 s and 18.87 s normal, so 3.8% against the two normal runs' own 2.7% spread (up to 15% on one scene); painted state identical in all. In fusain the same change halved a stroke, because its counts ran for every pixel; huile's in-loop counts do not. (4) Also seen: brush_step allocates about 92 to 105 arrays at every step (numba's NRT stats: 1.23 million in the painting scene, all freed). One allocation and free costs 20 to 60 ns here at those sizes, about 1.5% of a 400 us step; the rest is zeroing large arrays, which is work. Neither is worth a change. Compiling the counts out entirely (empty NRT_incref/decref) leaks every array and ran 54% slower, so it measures nothing.

title: Owner to try: white wax over heavy graphite, by hand, to settle how a waxy tip meets graphite crumbs
description: Since #82 (fusain-14f) a waxy tip rides on any bed of dust, graphite crumbs included. Over an 8B shaded at 0.95, a crayon lays 0.67 of what it lays on bare paper (was 0.12), and a white crayon there reads nearly clean white: luminance 0.58, against 0.18 before #82 (seed 7, cartridge; the comparison renders were made in the session of 18 November). On real paper burnished graphite is slick, wax grips it poorly and picks graphite up, so it probably reads as a dirty light grey (about 0.3 to 0.4): before #82 understated it, now it overstates it. The owner is to lay a firm patch of 6B or 8B, run a white crayon or white coloured pencil across it, and say whether it reads white, light grey or barely there. Then: leave it (white); or (grey, the likely case) a waxy tip rides on graphite but grips it less where it is polished and picks graphite up into the line; or (barely there) wax does not ride on graphite crumbs, keeping the bed rule for pastel and charcoal.
notes: Brought from fusain's tracker, where it was fusain-586 (github.com/joce/fusain, archived). Pull request numbers are that repository's; fusain is now murex.fusain, and its files are under murex/fusain/, tests/fusain/, docs/fusain/.

title: Calibrate graphite tones against scans of real pencil
description: The constants of fusain/_engine.py were set so that tones land near figures estimated from experience (docs/design.md, One step of a stroke), not measured. Scan swatches of real 4H, HB, 2B and 6B on cartridge paper at a few pressures and numbers of layers, and fit the constants to them.
notes: Brought from fusain's tracker, where it was fusain-fdh (github.com/joce/fusain, archived). The files it names are now murex/fusain/_engine.py and docs/fusain/design.md.

title: Keep the example images in Git LFS
description:
The histories of fusain and oilpaint came into this repository whole (murex-9r5.1, murex-9r5.2), and with them every past version of the example images: the repository went from 0.4 MB to about 490 MB, of which the images checked out are about 40 MB (examples/fusain/output 19 MB, examples/huile/output 18 MB, plus huile's reference photographs). Every change meant to alter the picture regenerates them all, so it grows with each one.

What LFS would do: every image, past and present, becomes a small pointer in git, and a clone fetches only the images of the commit it checks out. The server still stores everything, and LFS storage and bandwidth count against the GitHub plan's quota: check it first.

How: git lfs migrate import --include='*.png,*.jpg' --everything, then a .gitattributes that tracks them. It rewrites every commit from the first image on, so main is force-pushed and every clone and open branch is made again. With one user that is an annoyance, not a problem; it is cheapest before a history is merged, and the two histories were merged without it.

What it complicates, to settle before doing it:
- CI needs lfs: true on its checkouts, or the tests that read images get pointer files (huile's reference images, anything a test opens).
- raw.githubusercontent.com links to an image stop working (they return the pointer): a README shown on PyPI must link to media.githubusercontent.com or to the repository's rendered page. The README here links relatively, which GitHub renders with LFS.
- Every machine needs git-lfs installed. Not checked: whether a Claude Code cloud session has it and can reach the LFS endpoint through its proxy; if it cannot, the examples cannot be regenerated and committed from one.
- The source distribution and the wheel are built from the working tree: with pointers there instead of images, nothing the package ships may be an image (today nothing is).

An alternative that needs no rewrite and gives a clone most of the benefit: git clone --filter=blob:none fetches old versions of the images only when something asks for them. Try it first, and do the migration only if it is not enough.

Asked for by the owner on 2026-11-19.
acceptance_criteria: Decided, with the quota checked, whether to migrate or to rely on blobless clones. If migrated: a fresh clone fetches only the current images; CI passes with lfs enabled; the READMEs show their images on GitHub; a cloud session can regenerate and push an example image.
close_reason: Done. The images are in Git LFS on main (0ab8725), the whole history rewritten. Measured: a fresh clone of all branches and tags is 2.5 MB of git objects plus 40 MB of current images, against about 491 MB before; 503 image versions (532 MB) uploaded to LFS storage, within the free 10 GiB. Murex's first 12 commits (before the libraries) are untouched, so v0.1.1 and v0.2.0 stay on main; the 147 others keep their messages byte for byte, authors, dates and parents, every non-image file identical, each image a pointer to the sha256 of the original; their stale GitHub signatures were removed. The README's relative image links work (github.com/.../raw/ redirects to media.githubusercontent.com): all 39 files serve byte-identical to the originals. CI needs no LFS: 1818 tests pass with every image a pointer. tests/test_repository.py fails if an image is committed outside LFS. The old main (965ff90) is no longer on any branch. GitHub's own size for the repository drops only when it collects the old objects, which old pull requests still refer to.

title: spectral's numbers follow NumPy's own arithmetic to the last bit: between NumPy 1.26 and 2.x they differ, and nothing says they cannot again
description: Why NumPy 1.x gave other numbers (murex-dnn), measured on 15 November 2026 with Python 3.12 on x86-64: under NumPy 1.26.4, srgb_to_linear of a colour, SPECTRUM_TO_RGB and all seven rows of _BASIS differ from NumPy 2.0.2 and 2.5.5 in their last bits (the basis by at most 1.3e-15, a reflectance by 3.3e-16), and 2.0.2 and 2.5.5 agree with each other exactly. Everything in that path is double precision, so it is not NumPy 2's promotion rules: it is NumPy's own elementwise routines (the power in srgb_to_linear, tanh) and np.linalg.solve in _lhtss, which builds _BASIS at import, rounding differently from one build to another. Requiring NumPy 2 removes the difference that was seen, but the dependence remains: a later NumPy, another BLAS, or another processor (the SIMD paths of NumPy's ufuncs differ between x86 and ARM) may round differently again, and oilpaint checks its pictures byte for byte. CI runs Linux and Windows on x86 only. To consider: store _BASIS and SPECTRUM_TO_RGB as constants instead of solving for them at import; make srgb_to_linear's power independent of NumPy's ufunc (a numba kernel, as the other kernels are); a test that pins a few reflectances to the bit, run on an ARM runner too.
notes: 16 Nov 2026: _BASIS and SPECTRUM_TO_RGB are stored literals (murex/_spectral_tables.py; tools/derive_spectral_tables.py --check), and tests/test_bits.py pins reflectances and KM layers on x86-64 (murex PR #9). An ARM CI job (ubuntu-24.04-arm) failed 8 of those pins in the last bits, so it was taken out of #9: add it back with the fix. Cause: NumPy's SIMD power/tanh/exp and BLAS in the matmuls (weights @ _BASIS, reflectance_to_linear_rgb) round per processor; a numba power changes bits on 5% of elements. DECIDED by the owner (16 Nov): make spectral's arithmetic the same everywhere (deterministic kernels, no BLAS), a breaking change re-recording fusain and oilpaint. NOT NOW: first bring oilpaint's later engine changes into murex and make oilpaint depend on murex.
close_reason: Not doing. Identical bits on every machine was built and worked (joce/murex#19 for the colour science, merged then reverted; joce/murex#21 for the media, CI green on x86-64, ARM and Windows, closed unmerged), but it takes murex's own maths library (fdlibm ports, about 900 lines), NumPy's ziggurat tables for the random draws, and a ban on ordinary NumPy calls in murex's code. The owner judged that not worth it for this project. Pictures are checked to the bit on one machine; on another kind of machine the recorded hashes are skipped. AGENTS.md says so, and says not to bring it back unasked. The work stays reachable from joce/murex#21.

title: Require NumPy 2 and numba 0.60: srgb_to_reflectance differs under NumPy 1.26
description: Measured from fusain: the reflectance of a paper's colour (spectral.srgb_to_reflectance) hashes differently under NumPy 1.26.4 and 2.5.5 with the same Python 3.12, numba 0.68.1 and murex 0.2.0. The numbers must not depend on the NumPy installed. Decision (owner): drop NumPy 1.x; numpy>=2.0, numba>=0.60 (first numba to support NumPy 2).
close_reason: pyproject requires numpy>=2.0 and numba>=0.60 (confirmed on PyPI metadata); uv.lock updated; CHANGELOG and docs/release_next.md say so. No arithmetic changed.

title: _libm.power is three times as slow as the C library's
description: Measured in a numba loop: _libm.power 41 ns, x ** 0.3 (C library) 14 ns; exp 6 ns against 5. No measurable effect on huile's bench or fusain's benchmark (murex-9v4), but a kernel that raises per pixel would feel it. fdlibm's pow works out log2 in double-double; a table-driven version (as ARM's optimized-routines pow) would be faster and still IEEE-only. Only if a profile shows it.
close_reason: Moot: murex._libm and murex._random are not kept (joce/murex#21 closed, joce/murex#19 reverted; see murex-9v4).

title: huile: the pressure under a knife (Reynolds lubrication), for sideways flow and the blade's height
Rounding: places a last bit could still decide an outcome
description: Left open by oilpaint-nil, none seen to flip a mark in the sweeps (implementer 638 configurations, reviewer 184 marks), listed so that they are not rediscovered: (1) SAME_TO_ROUNDING = 1e-5 in _join_top_if_alike sits in a continuous tail of likeness values, not a gap: decisions near it can go either way (bench: 15 of 210,684 within 10% of it). A continuous rule would need a change to the layer model. (2) noise.lattice_noise sizes its grid with int(U.max()) from cos/sin products; flips only if a math library returns cos(0) != 1. Using whole_floor there changes the bench state. (3) The many '> 0' guards on volumes in _engine.py were not audited one by one. (4) Thin layers are ill-conditioned: a pixel's total differs by tens of ulps, which is up to 0.4% of a thin layer under or over a thick one (SCRAPER upright at x=80.5, angle 270, follow_path False, pressure 0.7); continuous, not a switch. (5) noise.canvas_weave parity was left alone as surface generation on generic values. Do nothing unless a real cross-machine difference shows up.
notes: Brought from oilpaint's tracker, where it was oilpaint-76t (github.com/joce/oilpaint, archived). oilpaint is now murex.huile: its files are under murex/huile/, and noise is murex's shared murex/noise.py, where a change to lattice_noise would also have to leave fusain's fingerprints as they are (fusain calls it).

title: make pre-push fails in a fresh clone: tox's spell env needs cspell before anything installs it
description: As in fusain (fusain-t6h): pre-push runs tox first, tox's spell environment runs npm run spell, and node_modules/.bin/cspell was a prerequisite only of the spell and spell-changed targets. In a fresh clone tox -e spell failed with 'cspell: not found' (exit 127).
close_reason: The tox target has node_modules/.bin/cspell as a prerequisite; in a fresh clone tox -e spell passes once it is made.
